1#א: Eating vessels. For it is written: every item that comes into fire; and there is no way to use fire except for needs of eating. Of metal, for it is written: only the gold, etc., and all mentioned in the verse is called metal. Glass too has the law of metal, since if it breaks it can be repaired by melting. And the reason for tevilah is so that they emerge from the impurity of the non-Jew to the sanctity of Israel:
1#ב: Or a spring of forty se'ah. Beit Yosef challenged what Tur wrote — it is not clear, etc., for regarding impurity too he ruled in siman 201 that we require forty se'ah; and Darkei Moshe resolved that Tur challenges according to the view of Sefer HaMitzvos, who wrote: even though a spring, etc. (end of his words), that according to him it suffices with less than forty se'ah for impurity, but he is stringent in this tevilah over that — our rabbi wondered why the difference. And it is not pleasing to me from Tur's wording, also from the law, for certainly Semak too holds that for a woman it does not suffice in a spring less than forty se'ah, but for an impure vessel it suffices with ten. And it appears to me the explanation of Tur's words is thus: this tevilah of vessels of a non-Jew we derive in the last chapter of Avodah Zarah from what is said "and it shall be pure"; and in truth there is no implication of "and it shall be pure" that it be through water — let us say through something else. Also what they said there that we derive from "only in the waters of a niddah" — there is no resolution in this, for the plain meaning of the verse refers to waters of sin-offering, as Rashi explained in the Chumash; rather we must interpret this "and it shall be pure," which is through water, since it is written regarding impure vessels "in water it shall be brought and it shall be pure" — from this we learn: in what do we find that this "and it shall be pure" regarding vessels of a non-Jew also refers to water? And after it is clarified that "and it shall be pure" refers to water, we interpret "waters of a niddah" as waters in which a niddah immerses, and it teaches us that it does not suffice with less than forty se'ah like a niddah, as stated in the Gemara. And in Tur we read "more than tevilah of impurity," and he means impure vessels; and this is what he says: since we do not know that purification is in water for vessels of a non-Jew except from tevilah of impure vessels, we do not be more stringent than them regarding a spring, except in what the Torah revealed regarding a mikveh, that it should be like a niddah:
1#ג: He immerses without a blessing. For the coating inside is only for ornament:
2#_: And specifically if he moistened his hand in mikveh water, etc. The rabbi left room here to defend himself, for his honor is in its place — he did not analyze this gloss at all, although they follow Mordechai at the end of Avodah Zarah, as we will quote shortly in the name of Darkei Moshe; nevertheless one must understand Mordechai's words and explain them as we will set forth, with God's help. First we will mention the essence of this matter that Tur and Shulchan Aruch mentioned — that rinsing one's hand in water helps — and this is what we teach in the mishnah, chapter 8 of Mikvaot: one who holds a person and vessels and immerses them — they are impure; and if he rinsed his hands in pure water, R. Shimon says he should loosen his hands so water enters them. And Rashi explained: he rinsed his hand before holding — pure, because moisture on his hand connects to mikveh water and there is no chatzitzah here. And likewise Tur brought in siman 197, and likewise at the end of Tur HaAroch. This is according to what we teach in chapter 6 of Mikvaot: one draws and moistens even a hair's breadth — meaning there one wishes to purify invalid water from valid mikveh water, and by moistening them a hair's breadth all invalid water is purified; and this halachah is widespread that moisture of a fingerbreadth to moisten helps to connect to a valid mikveh, as stated in chapter 2 of Gittin (daf 16). This is the intent of the mishnah we mentioned, that one who holds a person or vessel should rinse his hands in water — meaning before holding the vessel he should moisten his hands, even in detached water, and through their connection to the mikveh the water on his hand becomes actual mikveh water through hashakah; therefore the tanna and later poskim used the language of rinsing generally, like all rinsings that are in detached water — not like Rama, who explained Tur's words specifically in mikveh water; rather detached water also helps through hashakah. And what Darkei Moshe wrote in the name of Mordechai at the end of Avodah Zarah, that specifically mikveh water is required — this is Mordechai's language there: he also taught that one should be careful to immerse a glass vessel full of water and place it in a bucket full of water and sink the bucket in a pit, not to set it on its rim lest the weight of the vessel be a chatzitzah, but tilt it on its side and roll it in the bucket in the pit; and one asked: what is different from a person's foot spread on the ground in a mikveh, where there is no chatzitzah, because we say the water precedes the place before he puts his foot on the ground, as we teach in chapter 7 of Mikvaot: they immersed a bed in it even though its legs sink in thick mud — valid, because the water precedes. One might say: only in a complete mikveh where they are attached; but when one puts glass in a bucket, even full of water, it does not help because they are detached; and one should also be careful from what we teach in chapter 8 of Mikvaot: one who holds a person and vessels, etc. — end of Mordechai. From this Rama learned to explain here that the rinsing Tur mentioned is in mikveh water. In truth this is another matter: Mordechai deals with the weight of the vessel that interrupts the mikveh when it lies, and it is not applicable to say the water under the vessel is purified by hashakah from mikveh water unless there were already valid mikveh water under the vessel; then even though the vessel's weight interrupts so one might say those waters were completely cut off from the mikveh, nevertheless they remained connected and have connection on every side to remain in their validity — unlike detached water in a vessel, which you must purify through hashakah and create purity from the outset; for this a good connection is required, and since the vessel has weight it is not called a good connection. But in truth one who immerses a vessel in his hand in a mikveh does not need mikveh water on the hand; since there is no weight of a vessel, hashakah to detached water already on his hand with mikveh water is fine; nevertheless the person immersing must not grip the vessel forcefully, for then it is like the vessel's weight we mentioned — rather moderate contact, as they said regarding a niddah immersing in several places regarding her eyes and lips. This is Mordechai's intent: he also wrote one should be careful from what the mishnah says, one who holds, etc. — he asked: does the mishnah come to inform us? Rather it teaches that one must be careful not to grip too forcefully; for although the first tanna argues with R. Shimon, who holds he must loosen his hands, nevertheless moderate contact is required even for the first tanna, not with force — this is simple. And I saw in Mishmeres HaBayis of Rashba daf 190: we rule like the first tanna that he need not loosen his hands, only that he rinsed his hands first and does not press hard — tevilah is valid. And it appears to me Tur holds that if he grips moderately in his hand it is permitted even l'chatchila, and we do not decree lest he grip with great force and mikveh water connection not help; and this is why he wrote "however if he moistened, etc.," there is no concern — he asked: why "there is no concern" — he should have said permitted or it is fine; rather it teaches there is no concern lest he grip too hard. And Rosh is even more lenient, for he does not hold the vessel's weight interrupts and nullifies the connection of detached water on his hands with mikveh water; for he wrote in Hilchot Mikvaot: because the water precedes and touched the bed's legs before touching mud, and those waters are connected to the mikveh — therefore there is no chatzitzah, as we teach in chapter 8 of Mikvaot; and for this reason one need not lift his legs during immersion because the water precedes — end of Rosh. Behold he equated this law to rinsing hands, where the rinse-water is detached; nevertheless since Mordechai distinguishes between vessel weight or not, one should be stringent; therefore one who wishes to immerse a vessel should moisten his hands even in detached water, hold the vessel with moderate contact, and immerse it. One who wishes to immerse a vessel full of detached water in a bucket should draw water from the mikveh and place it with the vessel in water; then he must turn it on its side, for this is like a person gripping a vessel forcefully and immersing it — the person holding is voluntary and can hold without great force, unlike a full heavy vessel — unless the bucket is sunk in water and he lowers the vessel into it; then we are not concerned for vessel weight, since there is already valid water inside, as we said. And Levush writes that inside the water he passes it hand to hand; although that is a good method, for in that way there is no prohibition even if he grips hard, as Issur VeHeter wrote at the end of general rule 58 law 96 — nevertheless this is not the mishnah's method, which stated generally that he rinses his hands in water first; and Tur and Shulchan Aruch are not explained at all in that method, but in the method we said — and even detached water suffices, since there is no vessel weight and no gripping with force, tevilah is proper even l'chatchila; and even according to Mordechai we mentioned, who holds vessel weight is a chatzitzah, even if hands were moistened first in detached water, there is no concern here at all lest he grip with force, for it is a fixed halachah that we are not concerned for this even for niddah impurity, as will be explained in siman 198 seif 28, with Heaven's help:
3#_: He blesses on tevilat kelim. Darkei Moshe wrote in the name of Mordechai, chapter HaSho'el: some require blessing on tevilah of metal vessels so it not imply other vessels not liable for tevilah — end of his words; and likewise in Hagahot Ashiri — end of his words. I wondered: if so, he should also bless on metal eating vessels so it not imply vessels not for eating; rather one need not mention in the blessing all details of the mitzvos' explanations. And it is not comparable to Chanukah candle blessing of "ner" without specifying Chanukah, for there the essence of the mitzvah is Chanukah, as here with vessels; and covering blood with earth — we wrote the reason in its place that he blesses on two coverings. Therefore it appears to my humble opinion one should not change the custom at all; and afterward I found greater still at the end of Issur VeHeter in a responsum, and this is its language: but Mahariz Ronkel answered one should not mention "vessel," only immerse plainly:
4#_: Tripod. In foreign tongue "dreifus"; but fidleash means trivet in foreign tongue:
5#_: Slaughter knife. Mordechai wrote the reason it is not considered an eating vessel: it is forbidden to cut with it even cold; and although the animal is fit for eating, nevertheless it still requires cooking — end of his words. And likewise the skinning knife is not used to eat with as it is now — likewise Issur VeHeter. And it appears since Rama wrote on this "and good to immerse without a blessing," the same applies to iron implements for matzah that he wrote afterward do not require tevilah — likewise immerse without blessing, for one reason applies to both; only Rama wrote it here because Issur VeHeter wrote it in a gloss on this, and Tur listed scissors among vessels without eating needs — from the Talmud at the end of Avodah Zarah, where R. Ashi asked: even wool shears too? Rashi explained: scissors with which they shear wool garments; and the Gemara answers: eating vessels the Torah spoke of. And Perishah wrote Tur's scissors means even what they trim vegetables with. Maharshal disagreed and wrote he was not precise, for vegetable scissors are eating vessels, for in Choshen Mishpat siman 97 it lists tools for making food — end of his words. I say Perishah is correct, for at the end of chapter HaMekabel they say a butcher's resting-knife is for food needs, and Rashi explains it is butchers' knife for cutting meat — and see the skinning knife is also butchers' knife and does not require tevilah for the reason we mentioned; rather certainly "tool for making food" does not apply to eating vessels at all. The questioner who asked from wool shears could have asked from vegetables, but he preferred to ask; and furthermore Choshen Mishpat there lists slaughter knife, and here Mordechai and Shulchan Aruch ruled no tevilah is needed — Perishah's words are true. And Issur VeHeter wrote: likewise iron with which they fix kreplekh on Purim or scrape dough in the kneading trough — only if they remove burnt matter from bread when taking it from the oven requires tevilah — end of his words; and in all of them the reason is whatever the user needs cooking for does not require tevilah:
6#_: Wooden vessel that has, etc. Hoops in foreign tongue "reifen"; and Tur wrote in this law it does not require tevilah even for one who follows the stabilizer — meaning R. Meir in the first chapter of Shabbat: glass vessels that were pierced and lead was dripped in — R. Meir defiles because we follow the stabilizer, meaning the lead stabilizes the vessel for use — it is as if all lead; on this he said even R. Meir agrees here we do not say as if all metal, since use is not through that side:
7#_: Requires tevilah. Tur likewise wrote in the name of Sefer HaMitzvos and concluded: since one uses the silver inside, but not outside, even though it stabilizes; and some are stringent to immerse without a blessing. Beit Yosef explained his second way, which is primary in his view: a silver cup standing on a wooden vessel that surrounds and attaches it requires tevilah, as we say regarding a wooden vessel with iron hoops outside — but not outside, meaning if silver is outside and wood inside, even though silver stabilizes the wood like the wooden vessel with iron hoops that does not require tevilah; and "some are stringent" applies to both, whether silver outside stabilizing wood or the reverse, for we are uncertain whether we follow the stabilizer — such is his explanation. And to my humble opinion it is astonishing if Tur explained Semak thus, for then he should have ruled the same for iron hoops above, for Beit Yosef has one law for them — and he contradicts himself within the same breath, for he ruled immediately below iron hoops do not require tevilah even for one who follows the stabilizer; therefore it appears Tur explained Semak regarding vessel within vessel, as Semak explicitly states: silver vessel inside wooden vessel, where the outer is seen somewhat inside too; therefore there is a stabilizer like R. Meir in Shabbat chapter 1 above; only Semak holds we do not follow the outer stabilizer but the essence of use, which is a complete vessel only partly seen as outer inside; on this he said some are stringent when the outer is silver and fully stabilizes to immerse it, but one need not be stringent and bless; but in the first case where the inner is silver and use is essentially silver, certainly tevilah with blessing is required, for whatever is used inside — the stabilizer cannot nullify and exempt from tevilah; and in our Semak it explicitly writes "some are stringent to immerse where it stabilizes without blessing" — from this it applies only to this case; and so it appears from Shulchan Aruch here, who first wrote iron hoops do not require tevilah and then wrote silver vessel here requires tevilah — implying even with blessing; he retracted from Beit Yosef and holds "some are stringent" applies only to silver outside, as I explained; and Maharshal likewise; and not as Levush wrote that this tevilah Shulchan Aruch mentioned in seif 7 without blessing — rather it requires tevilah with blessing; this is clear. And not only that, but even in Tur's latter case where the outer is silver, since it stabilizes, tevilah with blessing is required, as Rama wrote in seif 10 "and if part of the silver," as I wrote there following those who go after the stabilizer — so here too; but for practical halachah I wrote in seif 10 one should not bless, neither here with outer silver nor there with part of the silver:
8#_: To cut cards. Beit Yosef wrote: likewise if he bought for commerce it does not require tevilah; Hagahot Ashiri concludes: since it is borrowed in his hand, Beit Yosef learned if he bought it requires tevilah, as Rama wrote shortly; but Issur VeHeter general rule 28 law 87 wrote: since if the first Jew wanted to use it for a meal, even temporarily, he would have had to immerse it — he is thereby obligated — therefore the second Jew borrowing from him must immerse it. I wonder greatly at Rama for not bringing this, neither in Darkei Moshe nor here; and one must say he immerses without a blessing; and likewise one who borrows vessels from a Jewish shopkeeper for a meal immerses without a blessing, only the shopkeeper should inform the buyer afterward not to immerse again with a blessing — as appears to my humble opinion:
9#_: And if not. In the Gemara we say: Mar bar Rav Ashi said: Father pledged a silver chair from a non-Jew, immersed it, and drank from it; and we do not know whether because he holds a pledge is like a sale, or because it appears the non-Jew intends to sink it; therefore poskim ruled: if we clearly see he intends to sink it, tevilah is required; and if it were not a doubt, it implies even if certainly he does not intend to sink it, there is doubt whether tevilah is required from pledge-as-sale; only Tur wrote: if one does not know whether he intends to sink it, we are in doubt, etc. — implying if certainly he does not intend to sink it, certainly no tevilah. And Beit Yosef writes: where he does not intend to sink it, we are in doubt, etc. — such is primary; and it appears Tur teaches a leniency that even whenever it is not known for certain that he intends to sink it, no tevilah is required, and all the more so when certainly he does not intend; and that he did not teach the reverse leniency that even when he does not intend to sink one may immerse without blessing — this is only a general stringency. And Maharshal wrote: when he does not intend to sink it, a Jew is forbidden to use it because of deceiving the non-Jew; he brought proof from Maharil's laws of Pesach, who wrote it is not proper to use any non-Jewish vessel before it is secured in Jewish hands unless permitted — therefore Tur did not permit here without intent to sink. I say: if there were prohibition of deceit, certainly intent to sink would not help, as pledge-as-sale — for with a Jew's pledge these things certainly do not help; and if there is prohibition with non-Jews, it would be like a Jew — why did Rav Ashi use a non-Jew's pledge without permission from pledge-as-sale? Also Tur and other poskim did not speak of one who transgresses; perhaps Maharil explained Rav Ashi used it with permission — then the question returns: why did Tur not write where certainly he does not intend to sink, for even when unknown there is prohibition from deceit per this view. Nevertheless it appears clear to my humble opinion there is clear permission to use a non-Jew's pledge without permission — it is no worse than canceling his loan in Choshen Mishpat siman 248, which was permitted [meaning in their days, since gentiles then practiced canceling Jewish loans, and Jews measured them as they measured them]. In Bava Kama (daf 113) Rashi explained this is not actual theft, for there is no desecration of God's name, for the non-Jew does not know explicitly that he lies, etc.; and what we say in chapter HaNezikin, Rav Kahana said "peace unto you, master" — Rashi: when he gives peace to a non-Jew he does not intend to bless him but his master (God). Tosafot wrote: requires study whether it is permitted because of deceit; likewise in Pe'ah; and above end of siman 117, forbidden to sell him nevelah as if kosher — that is not comparable here, for there he utters falsehood to deceive and receive good reputation or waive money for this lie, like theft from his purse — forbidden with non-Jews as with Jews; unlike here, where even if he could act justly and keep it all for himself there is no prohibition, since it is already in his hand permissibly for the loan; and see further siman 292 seif 2 regarding deceit of non-Jews if it is passive, as the non-Jew said. And I saw in great communities on Sukkot they use painted garments from non-Jewish pledges to decorate the sukkah and lend to many others, and likewise covers — Heaven forbid to say they all transgress; and in truth Maharil himself did not sign on this, only the copyist perhaps heard and erred — as appears to my humble opinion:
10#א: A Jew who gave silver, etc. Rama brought "and some disagree" — these are two views in Tur and Beit Yosef; Beit Yosef strained to explain, as he testified, that he explained everything follows the stabilizer, meaning the non-Jew stabilized the vessel — this is not "follow the stabilizer" in Gemara or poskim; and Maharshal explained Ritzba means the non-Jew gives silver needed for repair and disagrees with the law emerging from the first view, not the law itself; from this he wrote Rama was imprecise here — all this does not matter to me. What appears clear: this dispute is itself what Semag's gloss author disputed with Semag — Semag wrote the reason: the non-Jew's name is not called upon it, as Tur wrote; the gloss author wrote: it appears he means even if it did not hold a revi'it before; and Tosafot explained in Avodah Zarah because the vessel's essence is not the non-Jew's; therefore when it did not hold a revi'it before, the vessel's essence is the gentile craftsman for those who say we follow the stabilizer; and Ritzba explicitly wrote tevilah is required where it did not hold a revi'it — end of his words. Tur's intent is also thus: this is obvious if the non-Jew gives silver for the whole vessel — tevilah is required; if he gives a little in a way that stabilizes the vessel, this depends on the dispute of following the stabilizer, as Tur explained above in Sefer HaMitzvos; here he only comes to explain the dispute according to those who say a craftsman acquires through enhancement of the vessel, as Tur ruled in several places in Tur. The first view holds exemption when a non-Jew repairs depends on the reason the non-Jew's name is not called upon it — we require "his name is called upon it," as the mishnah's law; therefore no difference whether it held or not — even without holding a revi'it before repair, the non-Jew's name is not called after repair; and Tur teaches a leniency: if a Jew gave a non-Jew to repair a broken vessel and gives silver to repair, the non-Jew acquires enhancement of the vessel, that repair being slight — obviously no tevilah, for his name is not upon it. But even if a Jew gave silver to a non-Jew to make a new vessel with great enhancement and the gentile craftsman acquired it — one might have said tevilah is required; he teaches: since his name is not upon it, no tevilah. Ritzba disagrees and holds: since the gentile craftsman acquires through enhancement, whether he made a new vessel from Jewish silver with great enhancement, obviously tevilah is required; but even if the non-Jew has only a small repair, he acquires that enhancement and tevilah is required, since that small amount stabilizes — it is as if he gave silver for repair from his own, since he acquired it, and the vessel's essence becomes his — tevilah is required, as Semag's gloss author we mentioned; and we do not care whether the non-Jew's name is called upon it or not. This is a broad explanation with Heaven's help, without stumbling from all Beit Yosef's challenges; and Rama well ruled to immerse without blessing a vessel a Jew gave silver for, etc.; and that he did not bring even giving a broken vessel not holding a revi'it that Ritzba mentioned — because Rama did not decide like him, and perhaps this is included in making a vessel that Shulchan Aruch mentioned, that whatever does not hold a revi'it is not a vessel. And Maharshal wrote in vain that he was imprecise — rather he was precise. And what he wrote "and if part of the silver," this is from Mordechai chapter HaSho'el, brought by Beit Yosef: however if pierced below a revi'it and did not hold because of the hole, and he placed a piece of metal, tevilah is required, for we establish everything follows the stabilizer — end; and Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe explain it means the non-Jew gave the metal piece from his own — such are Rama's words here in this case only; and according to Ritzba we mentioned, the law is so even from the Jew's own, since he acquires enhancement and stabilizes; only Mordechai does not hold thus, therefore he required metal from the non-Jew. I wonder: Mordechai's words are regarding a broken Jewish vessel that did not hold a revi'it — when the non-Jew places his piece, he causes the vessel's essence; but when making a new vessel from Jewish silver and the non-Jew gives a little from his own, who says that little comes where it stabilizes? Rather say it is nullified in the majority of Jewish silver and is like all the Jew's, for everywhere we follow the majority — therefore this tevilah without blessing is meant; and so Rama's wording implies afterward "and likewise a Jewish craftsman," etc., immerse without blessing; and it is further proved Mordechai tied this ruling to what he ruled everything follows the stabilizer, and we already explained Tur in Sefer HaMitzvos concludes that because of what stabilizes one immerses without blessing — how can we say Rama ruled like those who follow the stabilizer to bless? Rather it is clear: since it is a dispute, one does not bless because of stabilizing, per "some are stringent" in Tur I brought above seif 7; therefore tevilah without blessing is required for outer silver above and here for part of the silver that stabilizes:
10#ב: He immerses it too without a blessing. Question: Issur VeHeter general rule 58 law 94 wrote: a non-Jew who gives silver to a Jew to repair a vessel for him, and the Jew buys it from him — even before it reaches the non-Jew's hand requires tevilah — end; implying even with blessing. And Rama's reason appears: Issur VeHeter's main reason obligating tevilah here is we do not say in this case "craftsman acquires through enhancement," as written there before — only regarding enhancement we say so, not the vessel itself, for the craftsman may not keep it; therefore the craftsman's name is not upon it; and since Rama saw other poskim hold "craftsman acquires through enhancement" as Ritzba we mentioned, he ruled here immerse without blessing. But what Rama wrote afterward "or he gave part of the metals from his own, no tevilah" — on what does this apply? If relying on "Jew makes for himself," obviously even if the non-Jew gave all metals he said first no tevilah; if on the previous "craftsman makes for non-Jew," it is difficult: since we are concerned perhaps here "craftsman acquires through enhancement," it becomes the non-Jew's vessel — what help that the Jewish craftsman gives part of the silver, since most of the vessel is the non-Jew's? This resembles buying a vessel from a non-Jew with a hole and a Jew repairs with Jewish silver — does that exempt non-Jew obligation? Now we hold the non-Jew's name is upon it — a fortiori from Rama shortly: if part of the silver from which the vessel was made is the non-Jew's, tevilah is required because we follow the stabilizer who is the non-Jew, even though most is the Jew's — all the more so if most is the non-Jew's and minority the Jew's. And further, even a stabilizer name is not here, for he makes a new vessel and is already nullified in the non-Jew's majority, as we mentioned — whence do we uproot tevilah obligation entirely? And even if you explain the non-Jew gives only part, it is still difficult: why above is tevilah required without blessing and here tevilah obligation is uprooted entirely? Therefore it appears there is a scribal error here, and this "or he gave part of the silver" belongs earlier; but if, etc., and it teaches two matters: first, if the non-Jew gave all metals, nevertheless he does not bless; and if he gave only part from his own, nevertheless tevilah is required. And so it appears primary to include this law in "requires tevilah without blessing," and there is no obstacle:
11#א: And he redeemed it — no tevilah. Maharshal wrote: even if he despaired of redeeming; but if initially he pledged with intent not to redeem and changed his mind and redeemed, tevilah is required — end of his words; and although above there is doubt regarding a Jew with a pledge from a non-Jew, here it is different, with proof from chapter Kol Sha'ah (Pesachim daf 31): there is a dispute whether a Jew acquires a pledge from a non-Jew; but a non-Jew from a Jew — all agree he does not acquire:
11#ב: A Jew whom they stole, etc. — no tevilah. Since he is not permitted to hold it publicly, the non-Jew's name is not called upon it; and even though this one despaired of it — likewise Issur VeHeter in the gloss:
14#_: We do not believe a minor, etc. Because tevilat kelim is d'oraisa; and if he immersed before an adult, tevilah is valid — Tur wrote the reason in Terumat HaDeshen: even for Rosh who holds a niddah immersing requires intent, nevertheless here an adult can teach the minor to intend to purify; and further, in this tevilah that is not from impurity to purity, who says intent is required? — end; and since Rama did not write here that the adult must teach him, it implies he adopts the latter answer that here intent is not required at all:
15#_: Their tevilah was valid. At first glance the wording implies b'dieved only, but in truth not so, for in the source of this law — responsum to Ramban — it is written: you asked whether to immerse vessels through a non-Jew — I have not heard this, but it appears permitted, for we do not say intent is required except for washing hands for eating, which is because of terumah concern — end; implying even l'chatchila permitted. That responsum is Rashba's; and in that responsum above he wrote regarding washing hands intent is required, or the washer's or giver's intent — nevertheless he was lenient for tevilat kelim even l'chatchila. And Maharshal wrote Rashba was lenient per his view that a niddah who immersed without intent — but for us who are stringent with niddah, we should be stringent with tevilah by a non-Jew; and through distraction in the text he did not look at siman 198 in Beit Yosef, where Rashba holds niddah requires intent; and behold Rashba is stringent even for washing hands for eating, yet lenient for tevilat kelim — all the more so more lenient than niddah. But I wonder how he can bless on what the non-Jew immerses while the Jew does nothing — therefore it is not proper l'chatchila; and therefore Shulchan Aruch wrote b'dieved language here; but if the Jew also immerses some vessel at that time while the non-Jew helps immerse other vessels, the blessing refers to what the Jew does — it is fine; and this is the responsum to Ramban we mentioned. So appears to my humble opinion:
16#_: He gives it to a non-Jew as a gift, etc. It appears to me this remedy is only temporary — for that Shabbat, or on a weekday while he has no mikveh; but after Shabbat or when a mikveh becomes available, since it is permanently settled in Jewish hands, it is certainly like purchased in his hand and no better than a non-Jew's pledge in a Jew's hand with intent to sink — tevilah is required. And furthermore regarding a borrowed tallit we find it is exempt from tzitzit for thirty days and afterward obligated, for it appears his own — so here too it appears tevilah is required after he can immerse, even with blessing; but since this is not explicit in poskim, one should be careful to immerse another vessel with it because of concern for a doubtful blessing:
